intro: Every price you pay is the end of a story. The $4.50 on a gas station sign, the $2 on a cup of lemonade, the $300 on a resold concert ticket: each one is the point where the people who want something meet the people who make it. Nobody in an office sets most of these prices. They come out of millions of choices by buyers and sellers, and they change when those choices change, sometimes by a few cents and sometimes by four times overnight.

This unit gives you the tool economists use most: the model of demand and supply. You will build a demand schedule and a supply schedule from small tables, learn the one difference that trips up most students (a movement along a curve versus a shift of the whole curve), and list the events that move each side. Then you will put the two sides together, find the equilibrium price, and trace what happens to price and quantity when a heat wave, a drought, a new machine or a viral video pushes a curve left or right.

Last, you will measure how strongly buyers and sellers respond to a price change, which is called elasticity. By the end you will be able to read a news story about any market, name which curve moved and why, predict which way price and quantity go, do the percent-change arithmetic that shows how big the response is, and explain why a concert ticket can resell for four times its face price while a gallon of milk never does.
bigQuestion: How do buyers and sellers, with no one in charge, arrive at a price, and what makes that price change?

timeline.t: Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations explains how self-interest leads sellers to supply what buyers want
David Ricardo argues that the cost of producing a good shapes its long-run price
Antoine Augustin Cournot writes demand as a mathematical relationship between price and quantity
The Chicago Board of Trade is founded, a marketplace where grain prices are set by bids and offers
William Stanley Jevons and Carl Menger explain value using marginal utility, the worth of one more unit
Alfred Marshall's Principles of Economics pairs demand and supply like two blades of scissors and develops elasticity
Friedrich Hayek describes prices as signals that carry information no single planner could gather
The federal government freezes most wages and prices for 90 days to fight inflation
Congress passes the Airline Deregulation Act, letting airlines set their own fares and routes

words.d: the whole schedule of how much of a good buyers want at each possible price
the amount buyers want at one specific price; one row of the demand schedule
when a good's price rises and nothing else changes, buyers want less of it; when it falls, they want more
the whole schedule of how much of a good sellers offer at each possible price
when a good's price rises and nothing else changes, sellers offer more of it; when it falls, they offer less
a change in something other than the good's own price that moves the whole demand or supply curve
goods that do a similar job, so buyers use one in place of the other, like tea and lemonade
goods used together, like printers and ink, so a higher price for one lowers demand for the other
the price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied, so the market clears
the amount by which quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied at a price below equilibrium
the amount by which quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded at a price above equilibrium
the percent change in quantity demanded divided by the percent change in price

test.q: A shirt's price rises from $4 to $5. What is the percent change in price?
test.why: Percent change is the change divided by the starting value: $1 ÷ $4 = 0.25, or 25%.

test.q: Movie ticket prices rise and theater attendance falls. In the market for movie tickets, this is
choices: a movement along the demand curve
test.why: Only the good's own price changed, so buyers moved to a different row of the same demand schedule.

test.q: The price of coffee rises sharply. What happens to the demand for tea, a substitute?
test.why: A pricier substitute sends some buyers to tea at every tea price, so tea demand shifts right.

test.q: Wages for restaurant cooks rise. What happens to the supply of restaurant meals?
test.why: Wages are an input cost. Higher costs mean fewer meals are worth making at each price, so supply shifts left.

test.q: At $2, buyers want 50 and sellers offer 20. At $3: 40 and 30. At $4: 35 and 35. At $5: 30 and 40. What is the equilibrium price?
test.why: At $4 quantity demanded (35) equals quantity supplied (35). No other row matches.

test.q: Using the same table, what is true at $5, where buyers want 30 and sellers offer 40?
choices: A shortage of 10, so the price rises
A surplus of 10, so the price falls
test.why: Quantity supplied minus quantity demanded is 40 − 30 = 10. A surplus pushes the price down toward $4.

test.q: A new video game makes a brand of headset popular, and both its price and the number sold rise. What happened?
test.why: Price and quantity moved in the same direction, upward. Only a rightward demand shift does that.

test.q: Perfect weather gives Illinois farmers a record corn harvest. What happens to the price and quantity of corn?
test.why: More corn at every price is a rightward supply shift, which lowers price and raises quantity.

test.q: In the same month, demand for a good shifts left and its supply shifts right. What do we know for sure?
test.why: Both shifts push price down. They push quantity in opposite directions, so quantity is indeterminate.

test.q: A price rises 10% and quantity demanded falls 30%. What is the elasticity of demand, and what kind is it?
test.why: Elasticity is 30% ÷ 10% = 3.0. A value greater than 1 means demand is elastic.

test.q: A store sells 200 phone cases at $10. At $12 it sells 180. What happened to total revenue, and what does it show?
choices: It fell, so demand is elastic
It stayed the same, so demand is unit elastic
It rose from $2,000 to $2,160, so demand is inelastic
It rose from $2,000 to $2,400, so demand is elastic
test.why: 200 × $10 = $2,000 and 180 × $12 = $2,160. Price and revenue rose together, so demand is inelastic.

test.q: Which good most likely has the most elastic demand?
choices: Insulin for a person with diabetes
Electricity for a home this month
One brand of frozen pizza among many
test.why: A single brand has many close substitutes, so buyers switch easily when its price rises.

test.q: Why is the supply of apartments in a city more elastic over ten years than over one month?
choices: Given time, builders can put up new buildings
Demand for apartments falls over time
test.why: Elasticity of supply grows with time, because sellers need time to add land, workers and buildings.

test.q: A storm shuts some refineries and gas supply shifts left. Why does the price of gas jump so much?
choices: Gas demand is elastic, so buyers leave
Gas demand is inelastic, so buyers keep buying as the price climbs
The storm shifts gas demand left
test.why: With inelastic demand, buyers barely cut back, so the price has to rise a lot to match the smaller supply.

test.q: A city adds a 10-cent tax on every bottle of soda that sellers sell. Which curve moves, and which way?
choices: Neither curve moves; price moves along the curve
test.why: A per-unit tax on sellers acts like a higher cost, so fewer bottles are offered at every price.

write.prompt: A popular taco truck near your school sells 150 tacos a day at $3. The price of beef rises and a new truck opens across the street. The owner asks: should I raise my price to $3.50? Use demand, supply and elasticity, with numbers you make up and label, to argue what she should do.
tips: Name each event, which curve it moves and which way (supply or demand, left or right).
Say whether the new truck makes demand for her tacos more elastic, and why.
Show total revenue at $3 and at $3.50 with the quantities you assume.
Name the trade-off: a higher price per taco versus the customers who walk across the street.
